newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU no campaign issue for anti-euro Germans-poll.
newsitem.headline: EMU no campaign issue for anti-euro Germans-poll.

text.p: Europe's single currency may be unpopular in Germany but it will not become a campaign issue next year because the pro and contra camps are not clearly defined along party lines, according to a leading pollster.

Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann, head of the Allenbach Institute and doyenne of German opinion researchers, said her surveys showed 52 percent of Germans were against the euro and this would not change much before the September 1998 election.

But, she wrote in her monthly report in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, this does not translate into an anti-euro movement because it does not fit into the voting patterns reflected with other issues in left-right splits.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl has vowed to see Europe's monetary union (EMU) launched in 1999 despite majority voter opinion against giving up the sturdy deutschemark.

This often seems paradoxical to observers unfamiliar with German politics, especially when popular politicians like Gerhard Schroeder, a potential Social Democrat (SPD) challenger to Kohl next year, are flirting with mild Euro-scepticism. "The idea that the monetary union must be an ideal campaign issue falls apart because there is no clear party profile among the supporters and opponents of the euro," Noelle-Neumann said in the report in Wednesday's FAZ.

"The relatively larger number of supporters can be found among the Free Democrats, the Christian Democrats and the Greens, while the opponents are more numerous among the Social Democrats and the Party of Democratic Socialism. But these differences are much to small to base a campaign on."

The opposition SPD failed miserably when it ran an overtly anti-euro campaign in the Baden-Wuerttemberg state election in March 1996. Most SPD leaders apart from Schroeder support a punctual start for the single currency.
Noelle-Neumann said the same party political logic meant the mounting calls in recent weeks for a delay in launching EMU would also not become a rousing campaign issue.

The post-war German system is a representative rather than a direct democracy, meaning that elected leaders are trusted to do the best for the country rather than seen as deputies whose legitimacy is constantly under question or review, she wrote.
"People... live with a kind of calculation about which decisions they want to leave to the experts or the politicians of their favoured party," she wrote.
"What then becomes important is which standpoint the voters feel has the strongest political will behind it."

Germans' have several fears about EMU, including the belief it will bring more inflation (48 percent) and more unemployment (35 percent). But the number of Germans expecting EMU to come has risen from 44 percent last August to 54 percent this May.

Noelle-Neumann linked this to a rising belief among German business leaders that EMU would start on time in 1999. Voters seem to have sensed the change in business leaders' thinking and adjusted their expectations accordingly.

Despite all the differences, German voters were still basically pro-European, she concluded. Asked if they would like to turn back the clock and abolish the EU, 55 percent said no and only 18 percent said yes.
